note: How each school ranks and uses the sources of law (uṣūl).

groups.origin: Abū Ḥanīfa (d. 150/767), Kūfa; Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad al-Shaybānī
groups.where: Turkey, Central and South Asia, the Balkans, the Levant, parts of Egypt and Iraq
groups.self: The school of reasoned understanding (أهل الرأي) built on the Kūfan Companions’ teaching, chiefly Ibn Masʿūd.
beliefs: Reasoning from causes, tested against strong general texts.
Strict conditions on single reports where the need is general.
Custom and juristic preference shape rulings.

sources: Qur’an, Sunna, consensus, Companions’ views, analogy, juristic preference, custom.
khabar: Not accepted against a general Qur’anic meaning, a matter of widespread need (عموم البلوى), or when its narrator acts against it.
maslaha: Not a named source; reached through juristic preference and custom.
dharai: Applied in practice, not named as a source.
urf: A strong source; rulings built on custom change with it.

groups.where: North and West Africa, Upper Egypt, Sudan, parts of the Gulf
groups.self: The school of the Prophet’s city, where the living practice of Medina carries the Sunna.
beliefs: Medinan practice is a transmitted Sunna.
The aims of the law (public interest, blocking harm) are real sources.

sources: Qur’an, Sunna, consensus, practice of Medina, Companions’ views, analogy, public interest, blocking the means, custom, juristic preference.
khabar: Medinan practice outweighs a single report against it.
istihsan: Accepted (attributed to Mālik: “nine tenths of knowledge”).
amal: A proof, ranked above single reports.

groups.origin: Muḥammad ibn Idrīs al-Shāfiʿī (d. 204/820), Iraq then Egypt
groups.where: Egypt, the Levant, Yemen, East Africa, South-East Asia, Kurdistan
groups.self: The school that first set out legal theory in writing (الرسالة), binding reasoning to the texts.
beliefs: Four sources: Qur’an, Sunna, consensus, analogy.
An authentic ḥadīth binds without further conditions.

khabar: An authentic single report binds; no extra conditions.
qiyas: The one accepted form of reasoning.
sahabi: Old (Iraqi) view: a proof; new (Egyptian) view: not. Disputed in the school.
mursal: Rejected unless supported, e.g. the mursal of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib.
urf: Only to understand wording and usage.

groups.where: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, parts of the Gulf and Levant
groups.self: The school of the people of ḥadīth: text and the Companions first, reasoning only as needed.
beliefs: Text and Companions’ fatwas come before analogy.
A weak ḥadīth is preferred over analogy.
Blocking the means is used widely.

sources: Qur’an, Sunna, Companions’ fatwas, a weak ḥadīth over analogy, analogy only by need.
qiyas: Used when no text or Companion view exists.
maslaha: Accepted when tied to the law’s aims.

groups.where: Historically al-Andalus; few followers today, wide influence through Ibn Ḥazm
groups.self: Taking the texts by their plain sense, without human reasoning added to the law.
beliefs: What the texts do not forbid is permitted.

sources: Qur’an, Sunna, consensus of the Companions, and the indicant within the texts (الدليل).
khabar: An authentic single report yields certain knowledge.

groups.origin: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (d. 148/765); al-Ṭūsī, al-Muḥaqqiq and al-ʿAllāma al-Ḥillī
groups.where: Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Lebanon, parts of the Gulf and South Asia
groups.self: The law of the Prophet’s House, as taught by the infallible imams.
beliefs: Reason is a source; analogy is not.

sources: Qur’an, Sunna (including the imams), consensus (as revealing an imam’s view), reason.
khabar: Accepted from reliable narrators (Uṣūlīs); Akhbārīs accept the Four Books broadly.
qiyas: Rejected, except analogy whose cause the text states.
maslaha: Not a source; reason fills that role.
sahabi: Only the imams’ sayings are proof.
mursal: Accepted from narrators known to narrate only from the reliable (disputed).
